```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(scales)
library(viridis)
library(knitr)
sf_use_s2(TRUE)
```

## The question

Where can a visitor find the best local food in New Orleans (Cajun/Creole, Seafood and Southern restaurants), and which part of the city is the best place to look for it?

I picked local food because that is what people actually come to New Orleans to eat. Steps 1 to 6 are below. Step 7 (reviewer adjusted ratings) and the final top 10 come next.

## Step 1 and 2: import and filter

The import is in [`R/import.R`](R/import.R). It reads the two Yelp json files with `stream_in()`, keeps businesses in New Orleans, LA whose categories include "Restaurants", and saves the result as rds. The review file is 5 GB, so that one is read 20,000 lines at a time and only the rows for New Orleans restaurants are kept. Details and the large data notes are in the README.

```{r}
restaurants <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/business_new_orleans.rds")
reviews <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/reviews_new_orleans_no_text.rds")

dim(restaurants)
dim(reviews)
```

`r comma(nrow(restaurants))` restaurants and `r comma(nrow(reviews))` reviews. Every restaurant has a latitude and longitude, which matters for the maps later.

## Step 3: pick the restaurant categories

The `categories` column is one string with commas in it, so first I split it into one row per restaurant and category.

```{r}
restaurant_categories <- restaurants |>
  select(business_id, categories) |>
  separate_rows(categories, sep = ",") |>
  mutate(category = str_to_lower(str_squish(categories))) |>
  select(business_id, category) |>
  distinct()

category_counts <- restaurant_categories |>
  count(category, sort = TRUE)

category_counts |>
  filter(category != "restaurants") |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Category", "Restaurants"))
```

"Restaurants" is on every row because that is how I filtered, so I dropped it from the table. After that the biggest categories are things like food, nightlife and bars, which are not really cuisines. The first real cuisine is cajun/creole at number `r which(category_counts$category == "cajun/creole")`, and seafood and southern are not far behind.

### Why these three

Cajun/Creole, Seafood and Southern are the three categories that describe New Orleans food. Gumbo, po-boys, crawfish, red beans and rice, fried catfish all land in one or more of these. They also overlap a lot in real life: a Cajun place usually serves seafood, and a lot of seafood places call themselves Southern.

```{r}
selected_categories <- c("cajun/creole", "seafood", "southern")

category_counts |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Category", "Restaurants"))
```

### Do they actually appear together?

```{r}
selected_wide <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories) |>
  mutate(has = TRUE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = category, values_from = has, values_fill = FALSE)

pair_counts <- tribble(
  ~pair, ~restaurants,
  "cajun/creole + seafood",  sum(selected_wide$`cajun/creole` & selected_wide$seafood),
  "cajun/creole + southern", sum(selected_wide$`cajun/creole` & selected_wide$southern),
  "seafood + southern",      sum(selected_wide$seafood & selected_wide$southern),
  "all three",               sum(selected_wide$`cajun/creole` & selected_wide$seafood & selected_wide$southern)
)

kable(pair_counts, col.names = c("Categories", "Restaurants with both"))

how_many <- selected_wide |>
  mutate(n_selected = `cajun/creole` + seafood + southern) |>
  count(n_selected)

kable(how_many, col.names = c("How many of the three", "Restaurants"))
```

`r pair_counts$restaurants[1]` restaurants are tagged both cajun/creole and seafood, so the overlap is real. `r how_many$n[how_many$n_selected == 2] + how_many$n[how_many$n_selected == 3]` restaurants have at least two of the three tags. That is the evidence the three belong in one group.

### Inclusion rule

A restaurant is in my group if it has **at least one** of the three categories. Requiring two would throw out most of the plain seafood places and plain Southern places, and those are exactly the kind of restaurant a visitor is looking for.

```{r}
selected_restaurants <- restaurants |>
  semi_join(selected_wide, by = "business_id")

n_selected <- nrow(selected_restaurants)
n_open <- sum(selected_restaurants$is_open == 1)
```

That gives `r comma(n_selected)` local food restaurants, `r n_open` of them still open according to Yelp. That is `r percent(n_selected / nrow(restaurants), accuracy = 1)` of all New Orleans restaurants in the dataset. I keep the closed ones for the counts and maps in this part, since the question for step 6 is where local food restaurants are, not where to eat tonight.

## Step 4: join the reviews

Filter the reviews down to the selected restaurants first, then join. No reason to carry the other `r comma(nrow(reviews))` reviews around.

```{r}
local_reviews <- reviews |>
  semi_join(selected_restaurants, by = "business_id") |>
  mutate(review_date = ymd_hms(date), review_year = year(review_date))

reviews_per_restaurant <- local_reviews |>
  count(business_id, name = "reviews_in_dataset")

selected_restaurants <- selected_restaurants |>
  left_join(reviews_per_restaurant, by = "business_id") |>
  mutate(reviews_in_dataset = replace_na(reviews_in_dataset, 0))

summary(selected_restaurants$reviews_in_dataset)
```

`r comma(nrow(local_reviews))` reviews from `r comma(n_distinct(local_reviews$user_id))` reviewers, from `r min(local_reviews$review_year)` to `r max(local_reviews$review_year)`. That is `r percent(nrow(local_reviews) / nrow(reviews), accuracy = 1)` of all the New Orleans restaurant reviews, for `r percent(n_selected / nrow(restaurants), accuracy = 1)` of the restaurants. Local food places get reviewed more than average.

One check: Yelp's own `review_count` column counts all reviews ever, while the dataset only includes a subset of them.

```{r}
review_check <- selected_restaurants |>
  summarise(
    yelp_review_count = sum(review_count),
    reviews_in_dataset = sum(reviews_in_dataset),
    ratio = reviews_in_dataset / yelp_review_count
  )

kable(review_check, digits = 2)
```

The two are close (ratio `r round(review_check$ratio, 2)`), so the review file and the business file were taken at about the same time. I use the dataset count from here on because those are the reviews I can actually look at.

## Step 5: check the city label against the real city boundary

Yelp's `city` column is typed in by whoever created the listing. The census has an official polygon for New Orleans. A spatial join tells me which restaurants labeled "New Orleans" are actually inside it. The boundary files were downloaded once with [`R/boundaries.R`](R/boundaries.R) and saved as rds.

```{r}
louisiana_places <- readRDS("data/boundaries/louisiana_places.rds") |> st_transform(4326)
new_orleans_boundary <- louisiana_places |> filter(place_name == "New Orleans")

restaurant_points <- selected_restaurants |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

restaurants_with_place <- restaurant_points |>
  st_join(louisiana_places, join = st_within, left = TRUE)

restaurants_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(city, place_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Yelp city", "Census place the point is in", "Restaurants"))
```

```{r}
n_inside <- sum(restaurants_with_place$place_name == "New Orleans", na.rm = TRUE)
n_outside <- n_selected - n_inside
```

```{r}
outside_places <- restaurants_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(is.na(place_name) | place_name != "New Orleans") |>
  mutate(place_name = replace_na(place_name, "none")) |>
  count(place_name, sort = TRUE)

outside_named <- outside_places |> filter(place_name != "none")
n_no_place <- sum(outside_places$n[outside_places$place_name == "none"])
outside_text <- paste0(outside_named$place_name, " (", outside_named$n, ")", collapse = ", ")
```

`r n_inside` of the `r n_selected` are inside the official New Orleans boundary. The other `r n_outside` say "New Orleans" on Yelp but the pin lands in `r outside_text``r if (n_no_place > 0) paste0(", and ", n_no_place, " of them are in no census place at all, so an unincorporated part of the parish") else ""`. Those are suburbs that use a New Orleans mailing address, so the pin is probably right and the city label is just loose. They stay in the dataset, but for the geographic comparison I only count restaurants inside the city, since that is the question.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Local food restaurants inside the New Orleans city boundary, colored by Yelp stars."
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = "grey95", color = "grey35") +
  geom_sf(
    data = restaurants_with_place |> filter(place_name == "New Orleans"),
    aes(color = stars), alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C", limits = c(1, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Local food restaurants inside New Orleans", color = "Yelp\nstars") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Almost all the dots are packed into the bend of the river on the west side: the French Quarter and CBD, then a thinner line going uptown. The whole eastern half of the city, which is mostly New Orleans East and the wetlands, has a handful.

## Step 6: choose and defend a geographic area

The question is "which part of the city", so I need to cut the city into parts. There is no one right way to do that. I compared three:

- **ZIP codes (ZCTAs)**, from the census. People know their ZIP code, but ZIPs were drawn for mail routes and some cover several very different neighborhoods.
- **Census tracts**, also from the census. Drawn to hold a few thousand people each, so they are small and even, but they only have numbers for names.
- **Neighborhood Statistical Areas (NSAs)**, from the City of New Orleans open data site. Named neighborhoods like French Quarter, Marigny, Bywater, Garden District.

```{r}
zctas <- readRDS("data/boundaries/zctas_701.rds") |> st_transform(4326)
tracts <- readRDS("data/boundaries/orleans_tracts.rds") |> st_transform(4326)
neighborhoods <- readRDS("data/boundaries/neighborhoods.rds") |> st_transform(4326)

# the neighborhood file's name column
nsa_name_col <- intersect(c("gnocdc_lab", "GNOCDC_LAB", "neighborhood", "NEIGHBORHOOD", "name", "NAME"), names(neighborhoods))[1]
if (is.na(nsa_name_col)) nsa_name_col <- names(neighborhoods)[sapply(neighborhoods, is.character)][1]
neighborhoods <- neighborhoods |> rename(area_name = all_of(nsa_name_col))
# the file has the names in all caps
neighborhoods <- neighborhoods |> mutate(area_name = str_to_title(area_name))

# ZCTAs cover the suburbs too, keep only the ones that touch the city
zctas <- zctas |> filter(lengths(st_intersects(zctas, new_orleans_boundary)) > 0)

zctas <- zctas |> mutate(area_name = zcta) |> select(area_name)
tracts <- tracts |> mutate(area_name = paste("Tract", tract_name)) |> select(area_name)
neighborhoods <- neighborhoods |> select(area_name)

city_points <- restaurants_with_place |> filter(place_name == "New Orleans")
```

The same join for each system. For every restaurant inside the city, find which area it is in, then count by area.

```{r}
summarise_system <- function(points, areas, system_name) {
  joined <- points |>
    st_join(areas, join = st_within, left = TRUE) |>
    st_drop_geometry()

  per_area <- areas |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    left_join(
      joined |>
        filter(!is.na(area_name)) |>
        group_by(area_name) |>
        summarise(
          restaurants = n(),
          average_stars = mean(stars),
          reviews = sum(reviews_in_dataset),
          .groups = "drop"
        ),
      by = "area_name"
    ) |>
    mutate(restaurants = replace_na(restaurants, 0L), reviews = replace_na(reviews, 0L))

  tibble(
    system = system_name,
    areas = nrow(areas),
    restaurants_assigned = sum(!is.na(joined$area_name)),
    unmatched = sum(is.na(joined$area_name)),
    areas_with_none = sum(per_area$restaurants == 0),
    areas_with_5_or_more = sum(per_area$restaurants >= 5),
    smallest = min(per_area$restaurants),
    largest = max(per_area$restaurants),
    per_area = list(per_area)
  )
}

comparison <- bind_rows(
  summarise_system(city_points, zctas, "ZIP code (ZCTA)"),
  summarise_system(city_points, tracts, "Census tract"),
  summarise_system(city_points, neighborhoods, "Neighborhood (NSA)")
)

comparison |>
  select(-per_area) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Geographic system", "Areas", "Restaurants assigned", "Unmatched", "Areas with 0", "Areas with 5+", "Smallest", "Largest"))
```

```{r}
cmp <- comparison |> select(-per_area)
zip_row <- cmp |> filter(system == "ZIP code (ZCTA)")
tract_row <- cmp |> filter(system == "Census tract")
nsa_row <- cmp |> filter(system == "Neighborhood (NSA)")
```

### What the table says

ZIP codes: only `r zip_row$areas` areas, and the biggest one has `r zip_row$largest` restaurants. That is too coarse. Telling someone "go to 70130" is not useful, that ZIP covers the CBD, the Warehouse District and the Lower Garden District, which are different places to eat.

Census tracts: `r tract_row$areas` areas, so the opposite problem. `r tract_row$areas_with_none` tracts have no local food restaurant at all and only `r tract_row$areas_with_5_or_more` have five or more. Most of the comparisons would be between tracts with one or two restaurants, which is noise. And nobody knows what "Tract 133" is.

Neighborhoods: `r nsa_row$areas` areas, `r nsa_row$areas_with_5_or_more` of them with five or more restaurants, biggest one `r nsa_row$largest`. The names mean something to a visitor and to anyone from here. Unmatched points are `r nsa_row$unmatched`, so the boundaries cover the city fine.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Number of local food restaurants per area, under the three geographic systems. Same color scale on all three."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5

count_maps <- bind_rows(
  zctas |> left_join(comparison$per_area[[1]], by = "area_name") |> mutate(system = "ZIP code (ZCTA)"),
  tracts |> left_join(comparison$per_area[[2]], by = "area_name") |> mutate(system = "Census tract"),
  neighborhoods |> left_join(comparison$per_area[[3]], by = "area_name") |> mutate(system = "Neighborhood (NSA)")
) |>
  mutate(
    restaurants = replace_na(restaurants, 0L),
    system = factor(system, levels = c("ZIP code (ZCTA)", "Census tract", "Neighborhood (NSA)"))
  )

bbox <- st_bbox(new_orleans_boundary)

ggplot(count_maps) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = restaurants), color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "sqrt", option = "D") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(bbox["xmin"], bbox["xmax"]), ylim = c(bbox["ymin"], bbox["ymax"])) +
  facet_wrap(~system, nrow = 1) +
  labs(title = "Where the local food restaurants are, three ways to cut the city", fill = "Restaurants") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"))
```

Same data, three pictures. The ZIP map is a few big blobs. The tract map is a mosaic where most pieces are empty. The neighborhood map shows the pattern at the scale people talk about: one bright strip along the river from the French Quarter through the CBD and into the Lower Garden District, fading out going uptown, and almost nothing east of the Industrial Canal.

### My choice: Neighborhood Statistical Areas

I'm going with the neighborhoods for the main analysis. Reasons, in order:

1. They match the question. "Which part of the city" is a neighborhood question. A visitor asks "should I go to the Quarter or Uptown", not "should I go to tract 133 or tract 137".
2. The areas are the right size. `r nsa_row$areas_with_5_or_more` neighborhoods have at least five restaurants, which is enough to compare averages without one restaurant swinging the whole area. ZIPs are too few and tracts are too many.
3. The names are documented. The city publishes the boundaries and the names are the ones on neighborhood association signs and in local news.
4. Nothing falls through. `r nsa_row$unmatched` restaurants inside the city are unmatched.

What the choice hides: a neighborhood like Uptown or the CBD is still big enough that the best street inside it matters, and the map can't show that. Also a few neighborhoods have one or two restaurants and their average rating will be unreliable. I flag those in the table below and will leave them out of the final ranking.

The requirement was at least 10 restaurants in at least 7 different areas. Under neighborhoods that is `r sum(comparison$per_area[[3]]$restaurants > 0)` areas with at least one restaurant and `r nsa_row$areas_with_5_or_more` with five or more, so it clears easily.

### Neighborhoods ranked by local food restaurants

```{r}
neighborhood_table <- comparison$per_area[[3]] |>
  filter(restaurants > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(restaurants)) |>
  mutate(average_stars = round(average_stars, 2))

neighborhood_table |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Neighborhood", "Restaurants", "Average stars", "Reviews in dataset"))
```

```{r}
top_nb <- neighborhood_table |> slice_head(n = 3)
```

`r top_nb$area_name[1]` has the most local food restaurants (`r top_nb$restaurants[1]`), then `r top_nb$area_name[2]` (`r top_nb$restaurants[2]`) and `r top_nb$area_name[3]` (`r top_nb$restaurants[3]`). Count is not the same as quality though. The next map shows the average Yelp rating by neighborhood, only for neighborhoods with at least five restaurants so one place can't drive the color.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Average Yelp stars of local food restaurants by neighborhood. Grey neighborhoods have fewer than five restaurants."

rating_map <- neighborhoods |>
  left_join(comparison$per_area[[3]], by = "area_name") |>
  mutate(average_stars_shown = if_else(restaurants >= 5, average_stars, NA_real_))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = rating_map, aes(fill = average_stars_shown), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", na.value = "grey88", limits = c(3, 5)) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(bbox["xmin"], bbox["xmax"]), ylim = c(bbox["ymin"], bbox["ymax"])) +
  labs(title = "Average rating of local food restaurants by neighborhood", fill = "Average\nstars") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

```{r}
best_rated <- neighborhood_table |>
  filter(restaurants >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(average_stars)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

kable(best_rated, col.names = c("Neighborhood", "Restaurants", "Average stars", "Reviews in dataset"))
```

```{r}
fq_stars <- neighborhood_table$average_stars[neighborhood_table$area_name == "French Quarter"]
fq_rank <- which(arrange(filter(neighborhood_table, restaurants >= 5), desc(average_stars))$area_name == "French Quarter")
```

Among neighborhoods with at least five local food restaurants, `r best_rated$area_name[1]` has the highest average at `r best_rated$average_stars[1]` stars, with only `r best_rated$restaurants[1]` restaurants, so one new place could move it. `r best_rated$area_name[2]` (`r best_rated$restaurants[2]` restaurants) and `r best_rated$area_name[3]` (`r best_rated$restaurants[3]`) are right behind. The big purple block in the east is one huge neighborhood with just enough restaurants to get a color, which says more about how big the area is than about the food. The French Quarter, with the most restaurants by far, is only number `r fq_rank` of `r nsa_row$areas_with_5_or_more` at `r fq_stars` stars. Tourist areas get a lot of reviews but not the best ones.

These are plain Yelp averages. Step 7 will redo this with reviewer adjusted scores and check whether the ranking holds.
